title: Position: Reliable AI Needs to Externalize Implicit Knowledge: A Human–AI Collaboration Perspective
claim: Only a small explicit, verifiable fraction of what AI learns is documented; the implicit majority drives capability but cannot be verified.
layout: 1 panel, nested concentric ellipses, outside-in, summary caption below
description: A single Venn-style diagram of three nested ellipses in muted beige and brown tones. The outer ellipse is labeled 'Data & Information' and holds faint italic examples such as conversations, code commits, draft versions, email threads, experiment logs and meeting notes. Inside it is a medium ellipse labeled 'Knowledge', listing bullets like reasoning patterns, problem-solving strategies, domain intuitions, debugging heuristics, failed experiments and intermediate steps. At its lower right it carries 'Implicit 80–95%' and '? Unverifiable'. The darkest, smallest ellipse sits at the upper left of Knowledge and reads 'Explicit 5–20%, papers, docs, DBs, ✓ Verifiable'. The eye goes first to the dark inner core. A bold takeaway line below says AI learns from both, but only Explicit is verifiable.
caption: AI training data spans data, information, and knowledge. Within knowledge, only the explicit fraction (5--20%) is documented and verifiable; the implicit majority (80--95%) consists of undocumented patterns that drive capability but resist verification.
abstract: This position paper argues that reliable AI requires infrastructure for human validation of implicit knowledge. AI learns from both explicit knowledge (papers, documentation, structured databases) and implicit knowledge (reasoning patterns, debugging processes, intermediate steps). Implicit knowledge remains unexternalized because documentation cost exceeds perceived value—yet AI learns from it indiscriminately, acquiring both beneficial patterns and harmful biases. Current reliability methods can only verify explicit knowledge against sources, creating a fundamental gap: the most valuable AI capabilities (reasoning, judgment, intuition) are precisely those we cannot verify. We propose Knowledge Objects (KOs)—structured artifacts that externalize implicit knowledge into forms humans can inspect, verify, and endorse. KOs transform verification economics: what was previously too costly to verify becomes feasible, enabling accumulated human validation to improve reliability over time.
